content: Thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins (TSI) or TSH receptor antibodies target the TSH receptors located on thyroid follicular cells, leading to increased production of thyroid hormones. Immunologically activated fibroblasts in the skin and eyes are responsible for the development of dermopathy and ophthalmopathy, respectively. Genetic factors play a relatively minor role in the pathogenesis of hyperthyroidism, with HLA-DR3 being the only well-documented genetic risk factor. Viral or bacterial infections can act as triggers for hyperthyroidism. This occurs because antibodies directed against the cell membranes of organisms such as E. coli and Yersinia enterocolitica can cross-react with TSH receptors. Excess iodine intake, either through oral consumption or exposure to iodine-containing radiographic contrast materials, can induce hyperthyroidism. This phenomenon is more common in individuals with pre-existing autonomously functioning thyroid glands or in patients with endemic goiter who are treated with iodine. This condition is referred to as the Jod-Basedow phenomenon. The anti-arrhythmic drug amiodarone contains a significantly higher amount of iodine than the recommended daily allowance, which can precipitate hyperthyroidism in susceptible individuals. Thyroid enlargement in hyperthyroidism can present as either nodular or diffuse. Gastrointestinal symptoms include weight loss, vomiting, diarrhea, and an increase in appetite. Cardio-respiratory manifestations include palpitations, angina, sinus tachycardia, and a widened pulse pressure. Neuro-muscular symptoms include nervousness, tremors, psychosis, and hyperreflexia. Dermatological features include increased sweating, palmar erythema, skin pigmentation, and alopecia. In the majority of hyperthyroidism cases, TSH levels are decreased or undetectable. This is the primary diagnostic test, as a normal TSH level virtually excludes hyperthyroidism. Serum T3 and T4 levels are elevated in almost all cases of hyperthyroidism. Iodine-131 uptake testing is not required for most patients but is typically increased in cases of hyperthyroidism. Thyroid peroxidase antibody levels are elevated in hyperthyroid patients, indicating an autoimmune component in many cases.
